newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian pepper prices heat up on supply squeeze.
newsitem.headline: Indian pepper prices heat up on supply squeeze.

text.p: A squeeze in world supply and growing demand from the United States have boosted Indian pepper prices, which are expected to remain high, trade officials and exporters said on Friday.

"The demand for pepper is growing and the supply is getting squeezed up, so whatever offers from any origin are getting picked up," said Taranth Vidyasagar, president of the Indian Pepper and Spices Trade Association (IPSTA).
Vidyasagar told Reuters by telephone from Kochi in the southern state of Kerala that the coming months would be crucial in terms of world pepper supply.
"Vietnam has marketed its produce, Malaysia has a crop of only about 10,000 tonnes and the United States has to depend on India until the Indonesian crop comes in August," he said.
India annually produces about a third of the world's pepper output of 180,000 tonnes. The other major producers include Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia and Vietnam.
India produced 62,000 tonnes of pepper in 1995/96 (November-October) against 55,000 tonnes in 1994/95. It has set a production target of 55,000 tonnes for the current year.
The country exported about 35,000 tonnes of pepper in the 1996/97 financial year (April-March) compared with 24,150 tonnes the previous year, officials said.
India's exports are targeted mainly at the United States, Europe and Japan.
"There is a global shortage for all varieties of pepper -- black and white," said G.A. Balakrishnan, a exporter in the southern city of Conoor.

"Chinese and Sri Lankan grades are not easily available. Indonesia is having problems with its supplies. Mexican grades are also in short supply and so the demand is high for the Malabar pepper from India," Balakrishnan said.
Pepper is used by meat packers, commercial bakers, pickle packers and condiment manufacturers.
Traders said the demand for pepper was picking up with mushrooming fast food outlets in the United States and parts of Europe.
M.R. Usha, deputy director of the state-run Spices Board, said pepper prices in April had risen to 9,950 rupees per quintal (100 kg) from 9,750 rupees in March.
IPSTA secretary P. Sethuram said pepper prices were currently hovering around 11,500 rupees per quintal compared with 8,500 rupees at this time last year.
Traders said pepper was contracted at 12,275 rupees per quintal for July futures, compared with 12,050 rupees contracted in March.
"Prices are not likely to fall very much. In the next two months after short covering is over, there may be a plateau and might stabilise around 11,000-11,500 rupees," Sethuram said.

A.S. Rajagopalan, an exporter, said 20 percent of India's pepper exports were in value-added form, which included oleoresins, essential oils, pepper in brine, dehydrated pepper, pepper powder, white pepper, dried pepper and sterilised pepper.
"Most exports in value-added form go to the United States," he said. "The (outlook) is bright."
